# Distances That Can Only Shrink: How Cube Labelings Refuse to Stretch

## A map that never lies in one direction

Imagine you are handed a complicated road network — a tangle of towns and
roads — and asked to redraw it onto the corners of a cube. Not a literal cube,
but a *hypercube*: a high-dimensional generalization whose corners are labeled
by strings of zeros and ones, and where two corners are joined by an edge
exactly when their strings differ in a single bit. Your job is to pin each town
to one of these corners.

You might expect such a flattening to distort distances wildly. Some towns that
were far apart could end up neighbors; some neighbors could be flung apart. The
surprising and clean fact at the heart of this work is that **a natural family of
such labelings can only distort distances in one direction.** They may glue
faraway towns together — taking *shortcuts* — but they can *never* push close
towns apart. In the language of metric geometry, these maps are
*non-expansive*: the distance between two labels is always less than or equal to
the distance between the original towns.

This is the **No-Stretching Theorem**. It is a small statement with a wide reach,
touching coding theory, the geometry of graphs, and the surprisingly rich
combinatorics of *partial cubes*.

## The cast of characters

Let us set the stage with three objects.

**The graph.** Start with a connected graph $G$: a set of vertices (towns) joined
by edges (roads). The *graph distance* $d_G(u,v)$ between two vertices is the
number of edges in the shortest path connecting them. Connectedness simply means
every town can be reached from every other.

**The hypercube.** Fix a dimension $k$. The $k$-dimensional hypercube $Q_k$ has
as its vertices all binary strings of length $k$ — equivalently, all functions
from $\{1,2,\dots,k\}$ into the two-element field $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$. Two
strings are adjacent precisely when they differ in exactly one coordinate. The
*Hamming distance* $\mathrm{H}(x,y)$ between two strings counts the coordinates
where they disagree:
$$\mathrm{H}(x,y) = \#\{\, i : x_i \neq y_i \,\}.$$
For example, $\mathrm{H}(0110, 0011) = 2$, because the strings differ in the
second and fourth positions.

**The labeling.** A *labeling* is simply a function $\ell$ that assigns to every
town $v$ of $G$ a corner $\ell(v)$ of the hypercube. We are interested in
labelings that behave gently along roads: for every edge $\{u,v\}$ of $G$, the
two endpoints either receive the *same* label, or labels that differ in *exactly
one bit*. Symbolically,
$$\ell(u) = \ell(v) \qquad \text{or} \qquad \mathrm{H}(\ell(u), \ell(v)) = 1.$$
Each step along a road flips at most one switch.

This single, local constraint — "each road changes at most one coordinate" — is
all the structure we need.

## Where such labelings come from

Why would anyone build such a labeling? The most natural source is an **edge
partition**. Suppose we sort the roads of $G$ into $t$ classes — perhaps by color,
by direction, or by some equivalence relation of our choosing. Assign to each
class its own coordinate. Now walk from a fixed home town to any town $v$, and
record, for each class, whether you crossed roads of that class an even or odd
number of times. That parity vector, read modulo $2$, becomes the label of $v$.

There is a subtlety: the parity vector seems to depend on which route you took.
But going around any closed loop returns you home, and the loop's class-parities
form a fixed pattern. Quotienting out by all such loop patterns — the *cycle
space* of the graph, expressed through a parity matrix $A$ over
$\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ — makes the label well defined. The result lives in a
space of dimension $t - \mathrm{rank}(A)$, and crucially, each road moves the
label by exactly *one* of a fixed family of directions (one per class), or by
nothing at all when its direction has been collapsed by the cycle space. One
step, one direction.

This is exactly the local gentleness we need. The honest target is the graph
whose vertices are the labels and whose edges connect labels differing by a
single one of those allowed directions. For the most natural partitions — in
particular the classical relation that groups edges lying directly opposite one
another, which recognizes the celebrated class of *partial cubes* (graphs that
embed isometrically into a hypercube) — the allowed directions are independent
coordinate axes and that target is the literal hypercube, with distance equal to
the Hamming count. In general the directions may overlap, and the target is a
slightly richer cube-like graph; the no-stretching conclusion holds all the same,
because its only ingredient is that each road advances the label by a single
step.

## The theorem, in three movements

The No-Stretching Theorem is proved in three clean steps.

### Movement 1: In the hypercube, distance *is* Hamming distance

The first fact is a satisfying identity: in the hypercube $Q_k$, the shortest-path
distance between two strings equals their Hamming distance,
$$d_{Q_k}(x,y) = \mathrm{H}(x,y).$$

Both inequalities are easy to feel. On one hand, *any* walk in the cube can only
fix one disagreeing bit per step, and the Hamming distance satisfies the triangle
inequality, so a walk of length $L$ cannot connect strings more than $L$ bits
apart — giving $d_{Q_k} \ge \mathrm{H}$. On the other hand, to travel from $x$ to
$y$ you can simply flip the disagreeing bits one at a time; each flip is a legal
cube edge, and after $\mathrm{H}(x,y)$ flips you arrive — giving
$d_{Q_k} \le \mathrm{H}$. Together these pin the distance exactly.

This is the bedrock. It converts a geometric quantity (shortest path) into an
algebraic one (counting bit differences) that we can manipulate freely.

### Movement 2: Walks map to walks without growing

Next, take any walk in $G$ — a sequence of towns connected by roads, from $u$ to
$v$. Apply the labeling to every town along the way. Because each road either
leaves the label unchanged or flips exactly one bit, the image sequence is a
legal walk in the hypercube (we simply skip the steps that don't move), and its
length is *no greater* than the length of the original walk:
$$\text{there is a cube walk } \ell(u) \to \ell(v) \text{ of length} \le (\text{length of the } G\text{-walk}).$$

The proof is a clean induction on the walk. The "same label" steps are free; they
shorten the image. The "one-bit" steps each contribute exactly one cube edge.
Nothing can ever lengthen the image. This is the precise sense in which the
labeling *contracts*.

### Movement 3: No stretching

Now the payoff. Take any two towns $u$ and $v$. Because $G$ is connected, there is
a shortest path between them, of length exactly $d_G(u,v)$. By Movement 2, its
image is a cube walk from $\ell(u)$ to $\ell(v)$ of length at most $d_G(u,v)$.
And the cube distance is the length of the *shortest* such walk, so
$$d_{Q_k}\big(\ell(u), \ell(v)\big) \;\le\; d_G(u,v) \qquad \text{for all } u,v.$$

That is the whole story. **The labeled distance never exceeds the original
distance.** Combined with Movement 1, this says the Hamming distance between
labels is bounded by the graph distance: counting how many bits two towns'
labels disagree on can only *undercount*, never *overcount*, how far apart the
towns truly are.

## Why one-sidedness matters

It would be easy to dismiss a one-sided inequality as half a result. In fact the
asymmetry is the point.

A labeling that is *isometric* — that preserves distances exactly — is a rare and
precious thing; graphs admitting one are exactly the partial cubes. Most graphs
are not partial cubes, so most labelings must distort. The No-Stretching Theorem
tells us *how* they are allowed to distort: only by collapsing. Every failure of
isometry is a shortcut, a pair of towns whose labels agree more than their
geography warrants, because some loop in the network folded two coordinates onto
each other.

This turns the gap between $d_G(u,v)$ and $d_{Q_k}(\ell(u),\ell(v))$ into a
well-behaved, always-nonnegative *defect* — a measurement of exactly how far a
given edge partition is from witnessing a perfect cube embedding. Because the
defect can never go negative, it behaves like an energy: it can be summed,
compared across partitions, and minimized. A partition with zero total defect is
exactly an isometric embedding; a partition with large defect has collapsed many
cycles.

## A bridge between fields

The construction quietly connects several worlds.

In **coding theory**, binary strings and Hamming distance are the native
language. A labeling that never stretches is a guarantee that a code built from a
graph's structure cannot accidentally separate codewords more than the graph
intends — useful when graph adjacency models permissible transitions.

In **metric geometry**, non-expansive maps into the hypercube are the workhorses
behind low-distortion embeddings, the tools used to approximate hard distance
computations by easy bitwise ones. The theorem certifies one half of the
distortion bound for free, leaving only the contraction side to control.

In **graph theory proper**, the result is the unconditional half of the theory of
partial cubes. The classical Djoković–Winkler relation sorts edges into classes
exactly as our partition does; the question of whether the resulting labeling is
isometric is the question of whether the graph is a partial cube. No-stretching
says: whatever else happens, you are never worse than the truth in the expanding
direction.

## The horizon

The cleanest open questions all concern the defect — the slack the theorem leaves
behind. Is the total defect of a partition computable from the cycle space alone,
counting exactly which loops the partition collapses? Is a graph a partial cube
precisely when some partition drives the defect to zero, and is there a unique
coarsest such partition? And if we color a graph's edges into a few classes *at
random*, does the resulting defect concentrate sharply around a value dictated
only by the degrees and the number of colors?

Each of these grows from the same seed: once you know distortion can only go one
way, the amount of distortion becomes a single clean number worth chasing. The
No-Stretching Theorem does not end the story of cube labelings — it gives that
story a direction.

# The No-Stretching Property of Hypercube Labelings Induced by Edge Partitions

## Abstract

Let $G$ be a connected graph and let $\ell$ be a labeling of its vertices by the
corners of a binary hypercube $Q_k$ — that is, by length-$k$ strings over the
field $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ — with the property that every edge of $G$ joins
two vertices whose labels are either equal or differ in exactly one coordinate.
We prove that such a labeling is **non-expansive**: for all vertices $u,v$,
$$d_{Q_k}\big(\ell(u),\ell(v)\big) \le d_G(u,v),$$
where $d_G$ is graph distance and $d_{Q_k}$ is hypercube distance. The labeling
can therefore fail to be isometric only by *contracting* distances (taking
shortcuts), never by *stretching* them. The argument rests on the elementary but
fundamental identity that hypercube distance equals Hamming distance, together
with a length-monotone push-forward of walks. The canonical source of such
labelings is the parity quotient attached to an edge partition of $G$: sorting
the edges into $t$ classes and recording class-parities of walks modulo the
graph's cycle space yields a labeling into a hypercube of dimension
$t - \mathrm{rank}(A)$, where $A$ is the cycle-class parity matrix over
$\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$. We develop the theory in self-contained form, give
algorithms for computing labels and the resulting distance defect, and discuss
the one-sided distortion as an invariant connecting partial-cube recognition,
low-distortion embeddings, and coding theory.

**Keywords.** hypercube, Hamming distance, non-expansive map, edge partition,
cycle space, partial cube, GF(2), graph metric, low-distortion embedding.

---

## 1. Introduction

A recurring theme across combinatorics, coding theory, and the geometry of metric
spaces is the attempt to represent the vertices of a graph as binary strings so
that graph adjacency is reflected by simple bitwise structure. The cleanest such
representations are the *isometric* ones, in which graph distance is reproduced
exactly by Hamming distance; the graphs admitting them are precisely the
**partial cubes**, a class with a deep and elegant theory rooted in the
Djoković–Winkler relation.

Isometry, however, is a strong demand that most graphs cannot meet. This paper
isolates the part of the story that holds *unconditionally*, for every connected
graph and every reasonable labeling. We show that as long as a labeling changes
by at most one coordinate along each edge — the natural local constraint shared by
all parity labelings — it can distort distances in only one direction. It may
contract, but it can never expand.

The result is deliberately minimal in its hypotheses, which makes it broadly
applicable. We require neither that the labeling be injective, nor that it be
surjective onto any subcube, nor that the graph be bipartite. We require only
connectedness of $G$ and the per-edge bound. In return we obtain a universal
upper bound on labeled distance, and with it a clean, always-nonnegative measure
of how far a labeling falls short of isometry.

### 1.1 Contributions

1. A self-contained development of the metric of the binary hypercube, including
   the identity $d_{Q_k} = \mathrm{H}$ (Theorem 3.4).
2. A length-monotone push-forward of walks under any edge-gentle labeling
   (Theorem 4.2).
3. The **No-Stretching Theorem** (Theorem 4.3): non-expansiveness of edge-gentle
   labelings on connected graphs.
4. A description of the canonical edge-partition parity labeling that supplies the
   hypothesis, and an interpretation of the resulting distortion as a defect
   invariant (Sections 2 and 5).
5. Algorithms for computing labels, hypercube distances, and the total
   contraction defect, with complexity analysis (Section 6).

---

## 2. The edge-partition labeling

We begin with the construction that motivates the entire development.

### 2.1 Edge partitions and the cycle-class parity matrix

Let $G = (V,E)$ be a connected graph and let
$P = \{E_1, \dots, E_t\}$ be a partition of its edge set into $t$ nonempty
classes. Assign to each edge $e$ the standard basis vector $\mathbf{e}_{c(e)} \in
(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^t$, where $c(e)$ is the index of the class containing
$e$.

Fix a base vertex $r$. For a vertex $v$, choose any walk $W$ from $r$ to $v$ and
form the **raw parity vector**
$$\sigma(W) = \sum_{e \in W} \mathbf{e}_{c(e)} \in (\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^t,$$
the sum taken with multiplicity and reduced modulo $2$; coordinate $j$ records the
parity of the number of class-$j$ edges traversed by $W$.

This raw vector depends on the choice of walk, but only up to the **cycle space**
of $G$. Concretely, any two $r$–$v$ walks differ by a closed walk, and the
class-parity vectors of closed walks form a subspace $\mathcal{C} \subseteq
(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^t$. Let $A$ be the **cycle-class parity matrix** whose
rows are the class-parity vectors of a cycle basis of $G$; then $\mathcal{C} =
\mathrm{row\,space}(A)$ and $\dim \mathcal{C} = \mathrm{rank}(A)$.

### 2.2 The quotient labeling

Passing to the quotient kills the ambiguity. Define
$$\ell \colon V \longrightarrow (\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^t / \mathcal{C}, \qquad
\ell(v) = \sigma(W) + \mathcal{C}$$
for any $r$–$v$ walk $W$. The target is a vector space of dimension
$$k := t - \mathrm{rank}(A),$$
and a choice of basis identifies it with the hypercube $Q_k$.

**One generator per edge.** If $\{u,v\}$ is an edge of $G$ in class $j$, then
appending it to a walk to $u$ adds $\mathbf{e}_j$ to the raw parity vector. Hence
$$\ell(v) - \ell(u) = \bar{\mathbf{e}}_j := \mathbf{e}_j + \mathcal{C},$$
which is either the zero coset (when $\mathbf{e}_j \in \mathcal{C}$, i.e. the class
direction is collapsed by the cycle space) or one of the class generators. The
natural target geometry is therefore the **Cayley graph** $H$ on the quotient
group $(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^k$ with generating set $\{\bar{\mathbf{e}}_1,
\dots, \bar{\mathbf{e}}_t\}$: every edge of $G$ moves the label by exactly one
generator. Running the push-forward argument of Section 4 verbatim with $H$ in
place of $Q_k$ shows the labeling is non-expansive into $H$,
$$d_H(\ell(u),\ell(v)) \le d_G(u,v) \quad\text{for all } u,v.$$

**The Hamming special case.** When the surviving class generators are *distinct
standard basis vectors* — equivalently, when each surviving class corresponds to a
single independent coordinate — the Cayley graph $H$ is precisely the standard
Hamming hypercube $Q_k$ of Section 3, and the labeling is *edge-gentle* in the
sense of Definition 4.1. This is the situation of the Djoković–Winkler relation
used to recognize partial cubes: when $P$ is that relation and the cycle space
collapses no surviving direction, $\ell$ is isometric and exhibits $G$ as a
partial cube. For a general partition the class images may be linearly dependent
(for instance, in a triangle with each edge its own class the three generators
become $\bar{\mathbf{e}}_1, \bar{\mathbf{e}}_2, \bar{\mathbf{e}}_1 +
\bar{\mathbf{e}}_2$, so $H$ is the complete graph $K_4$ rather than $Q_2$); the
labeling need not be isometric, and controlling that failure is the subject of
this paper. Sections 3–4 develop the Hamming case, which already contains the full
strength of the push-forward argument; the Cayley-graph generalization is
immediate.

---

## 3. The hypercube metric

We now develop the metric of $Q_k$ from scratch. Throughout, a vertex of $Q_k$ is
a function $x \colon \{0,1,\dots,k-1\} \to \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$.

### 3.1 Hamming distance

**Definition 3.1 (Hamming distance).** For $x,y \in Q_k$,
$$\mathrm{H}(x,y) = \#\{\, i : x_i \neq y_i \,\}.$$

**Lemma 3.2 (basic properties).** For all $x,y,z \in Q_k$:
(i) $\mathrm{H}(x,y)=\mathrm{H}(y,x)$;
(ii) $\mathrm{H}(x,y)=0 \iff x=y$;
(iii) $\mathrm{H}(x,z) \le \mathrm{H}(x,y)+\mathrm{H}(y,z)$.

*Proof.* (i) Symmetry of the relation $x_i \ne y_i$. (ii) The disagreement set is
empty iff the strings agree in every coordinate. (iii) Any coordinate where $x$
and $z$ differ must be a coordinate where $x$ differs from $y$ or $y$ differs from
$z$; hence the disagreement set of $(x,z)$ is contained in the union of those of
$(x,y)$ and $(y,z)$, and the bound follows from the size of a union. $\qquad\square$

Thus $\mathrm{H}$ is a metric on $Q_k$.

### 3.2 Adjacency and the hypercube graph

**Definition 3.3 (hypercube graph).** $Q_k$ is the graph on
$(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^k$ in which $x$ and $y$ are adjacent iff
$\mathrm{H}(x,y)=1$.

For a coordinate $i$, write $\mathrm{flip}_i(x)$ for the string obtained by adding
$1$ to $x_i$ (leaving all other coordinates fixed). Then
$\mathrm{H}(x, \mathrm{flip}_i(x)) = 1$, so $x$ and $\mathrm{flip}_i(x)$ are
adjacent; these are the only neighbors of $x$.

A key arithmetic observation in $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$: if $x_i \ne y_i$, then
$y_i = x_i + 1$, so flipping coordinate $i$ of $x$ removes exactly that one
disagreement. Formally,
$$x_i \ne y_i \implies \mathrm{H}(\mathrm{flip}_i(x), y) + 1 = \mathrm{H}(x,y). \tag{$\ast$}$$

### 3.3 Distance equals Hamming distance

**Theorem 3.4 (hypercube distance).** For all $x,y \in Q_k$,
$$d_{Q_k}(x,y) = \mathrm{H}(x,y).$$

*Proof.* We prove both inequalities.

*Lower bound $d_{Q_k} \ge \mathrm{H}$.* Let $W$ be any walk in $Q_k$ from $x$ to
$y$, say $x = w_0, w_1, \dots, w_L = y$. Each step is a cube edge, so
$\mathrm{H}(w_{i-1},w_i)=1$. By the triangle inequality (Lemma 3.2(iii)) applied
repeatedly,
$$\mathrm{H}(x,y) \le \sum_{i=1}^{L} \mathrm{H}(w_{i-1},w_i) = L.$$
Since this holds for every walk, in particular for a shortest one, $\mathrm{H}(x,y)
\le d_{Q_k}(x,y)$. (Inductively: a walk of length $0$ joins equal endpoints with
$\mathrm{H}=0$; prepending one edge of Hamming length $1$ raises the bound by at
most $1$.)

*Upper bound $d_{Q_k} \le \mathrm{H}$.* We construct a walk of length exactly
$\mathrm{H}(x,y)$ by induction on $n = \mathrm{H}(x,y)$. If $n=0$ then $x=y$ by
Lemma 3.2(ii) and the empty walk suffices. If $n = m+1 > 0$, then $x \ne y$, so
there is a coordinate $i$ with $x_i \ne y_i$. Let $x' = \mathrm{flip}_i(x)$. Then
$x$ and $x'$ are adjacent, and by $(\ast)$ we have $\mathrm{H}(x',y) = m$. By the
inductive hypothesis there is a walk from $x'$ to $y$ of length $m$; prepending
the edge $x \to x'$ yields a walk from $x$ to $y$ of length $m+1 = n$. Hence
$d_{Q_k}(x,y) \le \mathrm{H}(x,y)$.

Combining the two bounds gives equality. $\qquad\square$

Theorem 3.4 is the engine of everything that follows: it lets us replace the
shortest-path distance in $Q_k$ by the algebraically transparent Hamming count.

---

## 4. The No-Stretching Theorem

We now fix a connected graph $G=(V,E)$ and a labeling $\ell \colon V \to Q_k$.

**Definition 4.1 (edge-gentle labeling).** The labeling $\ell$ is *edge-gentle*
if for every edge $\{u,v\}$ of $G$,
$$\ell(u) = \ell(v) \quad \text{or} \quad \mathrm{H}(\ell(u),\ell(v)) = 1.$$

By Section 2, every parity quotient labeling of an edge partition is edge-gentle.

### 4.1 Push-forward of walks

**Theorem 4.2 (length-monotone image walk).** Let $\ell$ be edge-gentle. For every
walk $W$ in $G$ from $u$ to $v$ there is a walk $W'$ in $Q_k$ from $\ell(u)$ to
$\ell(v)$ with
$$\mathrm{length}(W') \le \mathrm{length}(W).$$

*Proof.* Induct on $W$. If $W$ is the trivial walk at $u$, take $W'$ trivial at
$\ell(u)$; lengths are both $0$. Otherwise $W = (u \to b) \cdot P$, where $u \to
b$ is an edge and $P$ is a walk from $b$ to $v$. By induction there is a walk $P'$
from $\ell(b)$ to $\ell(v)$ with $\mathrm{length}(P') \le \mathrm{length}(P)$.
Edge-gentleness gives two cases.

- If $\ell(u) = \ell(b)$: transport $P'$ to start at $\ell(u)$ (it already ends at
  $\ell(v)$). Its length is unchanged, and $\mathrm{length}(P') \le
  \mathrm{length}(P) < \mathrm{length}(W)$.
- If $\mathrm{H}(\ell(u),\ell(b)) = 1$: then $\ell(u)$ and $\ell(b)$ are adjacent
  in $Q_k$, so we may prepend that single edge to $P'$, obtaining $W'$ with
  $\mathrm{length}(W') = \mathrm{length}(P') + 1 \le \mathrm{length}(P) + 1 =
  \mathrm{length}(W)$.

In both cases $\mathrm{length}(W') \le \mathrm{length}(W)$. $\qquad\square$

The proof literally *contracts*: the "equal-label" edges are dropped, so the
image walk is always at least as short as its preimage.

### 4.2 Non-expansiveness

**Theorem 4.3 (No-Stretching Theorem).** Let $G$ be connected and let $\ell
\colon V \to Q_k$ be edge-gentle. Then for all $u,v \in V$,
$$d_{Q_k}\big(\ell(u),\ell(v)\big) \le d_G(u,v).$$
Equivalently, by Theorem 3.4, $\mathrm{H}(\ell(u),\ell(v)) \le d_G(u,v)$.

*Proof.* Since $G$ is connected there is a geodesic walk $W$ from $u$ to $v$ with
$\mathrm{length}(W) = d_G(u,v)$. By Theorem 4.2 there is a walk $W'$ in $Q_k$ from
$\ell(u)$ to $\ell(v)$ with $\mathrm{length}(W') \le \mathrm{length}(W)$. The
hypercube distance, being the minimum walk length, satisfies
$$d_{Q_k}(\ell(u),\ell(v)) \le \mathrm{length}(W') \le \mathrm{length}(W) =
d_G(u,v). \qquad\square$$

**Corollary 4.4 (one-sided distortion).** An edge-gentle labeling of a connected
graph is non-expansive. Its failure to be isometric is entirely one-sided: for all
$u,v$,
$$0 \le d_G(u,v) - d_{Q_k}(\ell(u),\ell(v)).$$
The labeling is isometric if and only if this defect vanishes for every pair.

The corollary motivates the central object of study in Section 5.

---

## 5. The contraction defect

**Definition 5.1 (pairwise and total defect).** For an edge-gentle labeling $\ell$
of a connected graph $G$, define the *pairwise defect*
$$\delta_\ell(u,v) = d_G(u,v) - d_{Q_k}(\ell(u),\ell(v)) \ge 0$$
and the *total defect*
$$\Delta(\ell) = \sum_{\{u,v\}} \delta_\ell(u,v),$$
the sum over unordered vertex pairs.

By Theorem 4.3 every term is nonnegative, so $\Delta(\ell) \ge 0$ with equality
iff $\ell$ is isometric. The defect is therefore a faithful, monotone gauge of how
far a partition is from witnessing a partial-cube embedding.

**Mechanism of the defect.** Each unit of defect arises from a closed walk whose
class-parities cancel: a cycle that the partition fails to "see" forces two
labels to coincide that geography would keep apart. In the quotient picture of
Section 2, this is exactly the collapse of a class direction $\mathbf{e}_j$ into
the cycle space $\mathcal{C}$. Thus the defect counts, with multiplicity, the
cycles the partition collapses rather than resolves. Making this heuristic into an
exact cycle-space formula is the first open problem of Section 7.

**Two extremes.**

- The *trivial partition* with one class ($t=1$) collapses every cycle of even
  parity; its labeling is a single parity bit and contracts maximally.
- The *Djoković–Winkler partition* on a partial cube achieves $\Delta(\ell)=0$ and
  realizes the graph as an isometric subgraph of a hypercube.

Between these lie all intermediate partitions, with the defect interpolating
monotonically as classes are merged.

---

## 6. Worked examples

We illustrate the theory on small graphs; each can be checked by hand.

**A path is isometric.** Let $G$ be the path $0\!-\!1\!-\!2\!-\!3$ with each edge in
its own class ($t=3$). The graph is a tree, so the cycle space is trivial,
$\mathrm{rank}(A)=0$ and $k=3$. The labels are $\ell(0)=000$, $\ell(1)=100$,
$\ell(2)=110$, $\ell(3)=111$, each edge flipping one fresh coordinate. The labeling
is edge-gentle and isometric: $\mathrm{H}(\ell(i),\ell(j))=|i-j|=d_G(i,j)$, so
$\Delta(\ell)=0$. Every tree is a partial cube in this way.

**An even cycle is isometric under the opposite-edge partition.** Let $G$ be the
$4$-cycle $0\!-\!1\!-\!2\!-\!3\!-\!0$ and let the partition place opposite edges in
a common class: $\{01,23\}$ in class $0$ and $\{12,30\}$ in class $1$ ($t=2$). The
single independent cycle contributes the parity vector $00$ (each class is

$\ell(1)=10$, $\ell(2)=11$, $\ell(3)=01$ — the four corners of $Q_2$ — and the
embedding is isometric. This is the Djoković–Winkler partition; both class
generators are standard basis vectors, so $H=Q_2$.

$\{0,1,2\}$ with each edge its own class ($t=3$). The single cycle has class-parity

$\bar{\mathbf e}_1=10$, $\bar{\mathbf e}_2=01$, $\bar{\mathbf e}_3=11$; they are
linearly dependent, so the Cayley target $H$ is the complete graph $K_4$, not the
Hamming cube $Q_2$. With labels $\ell(0)=00$, $\ell(1)=10$, $\ell(2)=11$, every
pair of vertices is at $H$-distance $1$, matching $d_G\equiv 1$, so the embedding
is isometric *into $K_4$*. Note that interpreting the same labels in the standard
Hamming cube would give $\mathrm{H}(\ell(0),\ell(2))=2 > 1 = d_G(0,2)$: the labeling
is *not* edge-gentle, which is exactly why the correct target is the Cayley graph
$H$. This is the canonical illustration that the no-stretching guarantee is a
statement about the generating set carried by the partition.

**A genuine contraction.** Label the path $0\!-\!1\!-\!2\!-\!3\!-\!4$ by the single
parity bit $\ell(v)=(v \bmod 2)\in Q_1$. Each edge flips the one coordinate, so the
labeling is edge-gentle and Theorem 4.3 applies; yet $\ell(0)=\ell(2)=\ell(4)=0$,
so $d_{Q_1}(\ell(0),\ell(4))=0 < 4 = d_G(0,4)$. Here the total defect is strictly
positive: the labeling contracts heavily, but never stretches.

## 7. Algorithms

We record the natural algorithms behind the construction, with complexity in terms
of $n=|V|$, $m=|E|$, and $t$ (number of classes); $k = t - \mathrm{rank}(A)$.

### 7.1 Computing the labels

Choose a spanning tree $T$ of $G$ rooted at $r$. The tree determines a label for
every vertex by accumulating class basis vectors along tree paths; non-tree edges
contribute the rows of the cycle-class parity matrix $A$, whose row space is
quotiented out.

```
Algorithm RAW-LABELS(G, P, r):
    fix spanning tree T of G rooted at r
    label[r] := 0 in (Z/2)^t
    for each vertex v in BFS/DFS order from r over T:
        let e = tree edge from parent(v) to v, class j
        label[v] := label[parent(v)] + e_j   (mod 2)
    return label   # raw parity vectors in (Z/2)^t
```

To pass to the quotient, compute a basis of $\mathcal{C}$ from the non-tree edges,
Gaussian-eliminate over $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ to obtain $\mathrm{rank}(A)$ and a
complementary coordinate system, and project each raw label onto the surviving
$k = t-\mathrm{rank}(A)$ coordinates. Raw labels cost $O(nt)$; the elimination
costs $O(m t^2 / 64)$ with bitset arithmetic.

### 7.2 Hypercube distance

By Theorem 3.4, $d_{Q_k}(x,y)$ is just $\mathrm{H}(x,y) = \mathrm{popcount}(x
\oplus y)$, computable in $O(k)$ time (or $O(k/64)$ with word-level XOR and
population count).

### 7.3 Total defect

```
Algorithm TOTAL-DEFECT(G, label):
    D := all-pairs shortest paths of G        # BFS from each vertex
    S := 0
    for each unordered pair {u, v}:
        S := S + ( D[u][v] - hamming(label[u], label[v]) )
    return S
```

All-pairs distances by repeated BFS cost $O(nm)$; the defect summation costs
$O(n^2 k)$. Every summand is guaranteed nonnegative by Theorem 4.3, which doubles
as a runtime sanity check: a negative term signals a bug in the labeling.

---

## 8. Discussion and future directions

The No-Stretching Theorem isolates the unconditional half of the partial-cube
story. Its value lies in turning the distortion of a labeling into a single
clean, always-nonnegative number — the contraction defect — that can be summed,
compared, and minimized. Three lines of inquiry follow naturally.

**A cycle-space formula for the defect.** We conjecture that the total defect of a
partition is zero exactly when the partition refines the canonical relation
grouping "directly opposite" edges, and that in general the defect is governed by
the dimension of the cycle space the partition fails to detect. The mechanism of
Section 5 makes the cycle-collapsing local and countable — one edge moves the
label by one direction — suggesting the global metric comparison reduces to a
bookkeeping of cancellations amenable to an exact formula.

**An intrinsic characterization of partial cubes.** We conjecture that a graph
admits a zero-defect partition iff it is a partial cube, and that among all such
partitions there is a unique coarsest one, obtained by merging classes whenever
the merge preserves zero defect. No-Stretching already supplies one inequality for
free; being a partial cube is then equivalent to closing the remaining gap, and
gap-closing is monotone under merging compatible classes, hinting at a tractable
lattice of "good" partitions.

**Concentration of random defects.** If the edges of a bounded-degree graph are
colored into a fixed number of classes uniformly at random, we conjecture that the
normalized contraction defect concentrates sharply around a deterministic value
determined only by the degree distribution and the number of classes. The per-edge
increment is an independent draw from a small abelian group, so labeled distance is
a sum of weakly dependent steps, exactly the setting where martingale concentration
is most effective.

Each direction grows from the same observation: once distortion is known to be
one-sided, its magnitude becomes a single invariant worth chasing.

---

## 9. Conclusion

We have shown that any labeling of a connected graph into a binary hypercube that
changes by at most one coordinate along each edge is non-expansive: labeled
distance never exceeds graph distance. The proof reduces, through the identity that
hypercube distance equals Hamming distance, to a length-monotone push-forward of
walks. The canonical source of such labelings — the parity quotient of an edge
partition — places the result at the foundation of partial-cube theory, where it
guarantees the one-sided distortion bound unconditionally and recasts the residual
distortion as a well-behaved invariant ripe for further study.

Let $G$ be a connected graph and let $\ell$ be a labeling of its vertices by the
corners of a binary hypercube $Q_k$ --- that is, by length-$k$ strings over the

  \dist_{Q_k}\big(\ell(u),\ell(v)\big) \le \dist_G(u,v),
\]

(taking shortcuts), never by \emph{stretching} them. The argument rests on the
elementary but fundamental identity that hypercube distance equals Hamming
distance, together with a length-monotone push-forward of walks. The canonical
source of such labelings is the parity quotient attached to an edge partition of
$G$: sorting the edges into $t$ classes and recording class-parities of walks
modulo the graph's cycle space yields a labeling into a hypercube of dimension
$t-\rank(A)$, where $A$ is the cycle-class parity matrix over $\GF$. We develop

resulting distance defect, and discuss the one-sided distortion as an invariant

\section{Introduction}

A recurring theme across combinatorics, coding theory, and the geometry of metric
spaces is the attempt to represent the vertices of a graph as binary strings so
that graph adjacency is reflected by simple bitwise structure. The cleanest such
representations are the \emph{isometric} ones, in which graph distance is
reproduced exactly by Hamming distance; the graphs admitting them are precisely
the \emph{partial cubes}, a class with a deep and elegant theory rooted in the
Djokovi\'c--Winkler relation.

Isometry, however, is a strong demand that most graphs cannot meet. This paper
isolates the part of the story that holds \emph{unconditionally}, for every
connected graph and every reasonable labeling. We show that as long as a labeling
changes by at most one coordinate along each edge --- the natural local constraint
shared by all parity labelings --- it can distort distances in only one direction.
It may contract, but it can never expand.

The result is deliberately minimal in its hypotheses, which makes it broadly
applicable. We require neither that the labeling be injective, nor that it be
surjective onto any subcube, nor that the graph be bipartite. We require only
connectedness of $G$ and the per-edge bound. In return we obtain a universal upper
bound on labeled distance, and with it a clean, always-nonnegative measure of how
far a labeling falls short of isometry.

\subsection{Contributions}
\begin{enumerate}
  \item A self-contained development of the metric of the binary hypercube,
  including the identity $\dist_{Q_k} = \Ham$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:cube-dist}).
  \item A length-monotone push-forward of walks under any edge-gentle labeling
  (Theorem~\ref{thm:image-walk}).
  \item The \emph{No-Stretching Theorem} (Theorem~\ref{thm:no-stretch}):
  non-expansiveness of edge-gentle labelings on connected graphs.
  \item A description of the canonical edge-partition parity labeling that
  supplies the hypothesis, and an interpretation of the resulting distortion as a
  defect invariant (Sections~\ref{sec:partition} and~\ref{sec:defect}).
  \item Algorithms for computing labels, hypercube distances, and the total
  contraction defect, with complexity analysis (Section~\ref{sec:alg}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{The edge-partition labeling}\label{sec:partition}

\subsection{Edge partitions and the cycle-class parity matrix}
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a connected graph and let $P=\{E_1,\dots,E_t\}$ be a partition of
its edge set into $t$ nonempty classes. Assign to each edge $e$ the standard basis
vector $\mathbf{e}_{c(e)} \in (\GF)^t$, where $c(e)$ is the index of the class
containing $e$.

Fix a base vertex $r$. For a vertex $v$, choose any walk $W$ from $r$ to $v$ and
form the \emph{raw parity vector}
\[
  \sigma(W) = \sum_{e \in W} \mathbf{e}_{c(e)} \in (\GF)^t,
\]
the sum taken with multiplicity and reduced modulo $2$; coordinate $j$ records the
parity of the number of class-$j$ edges traversed by $W$.

This raw vector depends on the choice of walk, but only up to the \emph{cycle
space} of $G$. Any two $r$--$v$ walks differ by a closed walk, and the
class-parity vectors of closed walks form a subspace $\mathcal{C} \subseteq
(\GF)^t$. Let $A$ be the \emph{cycle-class parity matrix} whose rows are the
class-parity vectors of a cycle basis of $G$; then $\mathcal{C} =
\mathrm{rowspace}(A)$ and $\dim \mathcal{C} = \rank(A)$.

\subsection{The quotient labeling}
Passing to the quotient removes the ambiguity. Define
\[
  \ell \colon V \to (\GF)^t/\mathcal{C}, \qquad \ell(v) = \sigma(W) + \mathcal{C}
\]
for any $r$--$v$ walk $W$. The target is a vector space of dimension
\[
  k := t - \rank(A),
\]
and a choice of basis identifies it with the hypercube $Q_k$.

\paragraph{One generator per edge.} If $\{u,v\}$ is an edge in class $j$, then
appending it to a walk to $u$ adds $\mathbf{e}_j$ to the raw parity vector, so
$\ell(v)-\ell(u) = \bar{\mathbf{e}}_j := \mathbf{e}_j + \mathcal{C}$ is either the
zero coset (when $\mathbf{e}_j \in \mathcal{C}$) or one of the class generators.
The natural target geometry is therefore the \emph{Cayley graph} $H$ on the
quotient group $(\GF)^k$ with generating set $\{\bar{\mathbf{e}}_1,\dots,
\bar{\mathbf{e}}_t\}$: every edge of $G$ moves the label by exactly one generator,
so the push-forward argument of Section~\ref{sec:nostretch} (run with $H$ in place
of $Q_k$) gives $\dist_H(\ell(u),\ell(v)) \le \dist_G(u,v)$ for all $u,v$.

\paragraph{The Hamming special case.} When the surviving class generators are
distinct standard basis vectors --- each surviving class an independent coordinate
--- the Cayley graph $H$ is exactly the standard Hamming hypercube $Q_k$, and the
labeling is \emph{edge-gentle} in the sense of Section~\ref{sec:nostretch}. This is the Djokovi\'c--Winkler
relation used to recognize partial cubes: when $P$ is that relation and the cycle
space collapses no surviving direction, $\ell$ is isometric and exhibits $G$ as a
partial cube. For a general partition the class images may be dependent (in a
triangle with each edge its own class the generators are $\bar{\mathbf{e}}_1,
\bar{\mathbf{e}}_2,\bar{\mathbf{e}}_1+\bar{\mathbf{e}}_2$, so $H$ is $K_4$, not
$Q_2$), the labeling need not be isometric, and controlling that failure is our
aim. The next sections develop the Hamming case, which carries the full strength
of the argument; the Cayley generalization is immediate.

\section{The hypercube metric}

A vertex of $Q_k$ is a function $x\colon\{0,1,\dots,k-1\}\to\GF$.

\begin{definition}[Hamming distance]
For $x,y\in Q_k$, $\ \Ham(x,y) = \#\{\, i : x_i \neq y_i \,\}.$
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[basic properties]\label{lem:ham}
For all $x,y,z\in Q_k$:
(i) $\Ham(x,y)=\Ham(y,x)$;
(ii) $\Ham(x,y)=0 \iff x=y$;
(iii) $\Ham(x,z) \le \Ham(x,y)+\Ham(y,z)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
(i) follows from symmetry of the relation $x_i\neq y_i$. (ii) The disagreement set
is empty iff the strings agree everywhere. (iii) Any coordinate where $x$ and $z$
differ is one where $x$ differs from $y$ or $y$ differs from $z$, so the
disagreement set of $(x,z)$ is contained in the union of those of $(x,y)$ and
$(y,z)$; the bound follows from the size of a union.
\end{proof}

Thus $\Ham$ is a metric on $Q_k$.

\begin{definition}[hypercube graph]
$Q_k$ is the graph on $(\GF)^k$ in which $x$ and $y$ are adjacent iff
$\Ham(x,y)=1$.
\end{definition}

For a coordinate $i$, let $\flip_i(x)$ add $1$ to $x_i$ and fix all other
coordinates. Then $\Ham(x,\flip_i(x))=1$, and these flips give all neighbors of
$x$. Over $\GF$, if $x_i\neq y_i$ then $y_i = x_i+1$, so flipping coordinate $i$ of
$x$ removes exactly that disagreement:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:flip}
  x_i\neq y_i \implies \Ham(\flip_i(x),y) + 1 = \Ham(x,y).
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[hypercube distance]\label{thm:cube-dist}
For all $x,y\in Q_k$, $\ \dist_{Q_k}(x,y) = \Ham(x,y).$
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
\emph{Lower bound.} Let $W$ be a walk $x=w_0,w_1,\dots,w_L=y$ in $Q_k$. Each step
is a cube edge, so $\Ham(w_{i-1},w_i)=1$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:ham}(iii),
$\Ham(x,y)\le\sum_{i=1}^L \Ham(w_{i-1},w_i)=L$. Taking $W$ shortest gives
$\Ham(x,y)\le \dist_{Q_k}(x,y)$.

\emph{Upper bound.} Induct on $n=\Ham(x,y)$. If $n=0$ then $x=y$ and the empty
walk works. If $n=m+1>0$ then $x\neq y$, so some coordinate $i$ has $x_i\neq y_i$;
set $x'=\flip_i(x)$. Then $x,x'$ are adjacent and, by~\eqref{eq:flip},
$\Ham(x',y)=m$. By induction there is a walk $x'\to y$ of length $m$; prepending
$x\to x'$ gives a walk $x\to y$ of length $m+1=n$. Hence $\dist_{Q_k}(x,y)\le
\Ham(x,y)$.

Combining the two bounds yields equality.
\end{proof}

\section{The No-Stretching Theorem}\label{sec:nostretch}

Fix a connected graph $G=(V,E)$ and a labeling $\ell\colon V\to Q_k$.

\begin{definition}[edge-gentle labeling]
$\ell$ is \emph{edge-gentle} if for every edge $\{u,v\}$ of $G$,
\[
  \ell(u)=\ell(v) \quad\text{or}\quad \Ham(\ell(u),\ell(v))=1.
\]
\end{definition}

Every parity quotient labeling of an edge partition is edge-gentle
(Section~\ref{sec:partition}).

\begin{theorem}[length-monotone image walk]\label{thm:image-walk}
Let $\ell$ be edge-gentle. For every walk $W$ in $G$ from $u$ to $v$ there is a
walk $W'$ in $Q_k$ from $\ell(u)$ to $\ell(v)$ with
$\mathrm{length}(W')\le\mathrm{length}(W)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Induct on $W$. If $W$ is trivial at $u$, take $W'$ trivial at $\ell(u)$. Otherwise
$W=(u\to b)\cdot P$ with $P$ a walk $b\to v$. By induction there is $P'$ from
$\ell(b)$ to $\ell(v)$ with $\mathrm{length}(P')\le\mathrm{length}(P)$.
If $\ell(u)=\ell(b)$, transport $P'$ to start at $\ell(u)$; its length is unchanged
and still bounded by $\mathrm{length}(W)$. If $\Ham(\ell(u),\ell(b))=1$, then
$\ell(u),\ell(b)$ are adjacent in $Q_k$, so prepend that edge to $P'$ to get $W'$
with $\mathrm{length}(W')=\mathrm{length}(P')+1\le\mathrm{length}(P)+1=
\mathrm{length}(W)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[No-Stretching Theorem]\label{thm:no-stretch}
Let $G$ be connected and $\ell\colon V\to Q_k$ edge-gentle. Then for all $u,v\in
V$,
\[
  \dist_{Q_k}\big(\ell(u),\ell(v)\big) \le \dist_G(u,v).
\]
Equivalently, by Theorem~\ref{thm:cube-dist}, $\Ham(\ell(u),\ell(v))\le
\dist_G(u,v)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By connectedness there is a geodesic walk $W$ from $u$ to $v$ with
$\mathrm{length}(W)=\dist_G(u,v)$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:image-walk} there is a walk
$W'$ in $Q_k$ from $\ell(u)$ to $\ell(v)$ with
$\mathrm{length}(W')\le\mathrm{length}(W)$. Since $\dist_{Q_k}$ is the minimum walk
length,
\[
  \dist_{Q_k}(\ell(u),\ell(v))\le\mathrm{length}(W')\le\mathrm{length}(W)=
  \dist_G(u,v). \qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[one-sided distortion]
An edge-gentle labeling of a connected graph is non-expansive, and its failure to
be isometric is one-sided: $0\le \dist_G(u,v)-\dist_{Q_k}(\ell(u),\ell(v))$ for
all $u,v$, with the labeling isometric iff this defect vanishes for every pair.
\end{corollary}

\section{The contraction defect}\label{sec:defect}

\begin{definition}[pairwise and total defect]
For an edge-gentle labeling $\ell$ of a connected $G$, set the pairwise defect
$\delta_\ell(u,v)=\dist_G(u,v)-\dist_{Q_k}(\ell(u),\ell(v))\ge 0$ and the total
defect $\Delta(\ell)=\sum_{\{u,v\}}\delta_\ell(u,v)$.
\end{definition}

By Theorem~\ref{thm:no-stretch} every term is nonnegative, so $\Delta(\ell)\ge 0$,
with equality iff $\ell$ is isometric. The defect is a faithful, monotone gauge of
how far a partition is from witnessing a partial-cube embedding.

\paragraph{Mechanism.} Each unit of defect arises from a closed walk whose
class-parities cancel: a cycle the partition fails to ``see'' forces two labels to
coincide that geography would keep apart. In the quotient picture this is the
collapse of a class direction $\mathbf{e}_j$ into $\mathcal{C}$. Thus the defect
counts, with multiplicity, the cycles the partition collapses rather than
resolves.

\paragraph{Extremes.} The trivial one-class partition contracts maximally to a
single parity bit; the Djokovi\'c--Winkler partition on a partial cube achieves
$\Delta(\ell)=0$. Intermediate partitions interpolate monotonically as classes
merge.

\section{Worked examples}

We illustrate the theory on small graphs; each can be checked by hand.

\paragraph{A path is isometric.} For the path $0\!-\!1\!-\!2\!-\!3$ with each edge
in its own class ($t=3$), the cycle space is trivial, so $k=3$ and the labels are
$000,100,110,111$, each edge flipping a fresh coordinate. The labeling is
edge-gentle and isometric, $\Ham(\ell(i),\ell(j))=|i-j|=\dist_G(i,j)$, with
$\Delta(\ell)=0$; every tree is a partial cube this way.

\paragraph{An even cycle.} For $C_4 = 0\!-\!1\!-\!2\!-\!3\!-\!0$ with opposite edges
paired ($\{01,23\}$ in class $0$, $\{12,30\}$ in class $1$, $t=2$), the single
cycle crosses each class twice, so $\rank(A)=0$, $k=2$, and the labels
$00,10,11,01$ are the corners of $Q_2$: an isometric embedding. Both class
generators are standard basis vectors, so $H=Q_2$. This is the Djokovi\'c--Winkler
partition.

\paragraph{A triangle, with target $K_4$.} For $K_3$ with each edge its own class
($t=3$), the single cycle has class-parity $111$, so $\rank(A)=1$ and $k=2$. The
generators $\bar{\mathbf e}_1=10,\ \bar{\mathbf e}_2=01,\ \bar{\mathbf e}_3=11$
are dependent, so $H=K_4$, not $Q_2$. With labels $00,10,11$ all pairs are at
$H$-distance $1=\dist_G$, an isometric embedding into $K_4$. In the standard
Hamming cube the same labels give $\Ham(00,11)=2>1$, so the labeling is
\emph{not} edge-gentle --- precisely why the correct target is the Cayley graph.

\paragraph{A genuine contraction.} Label $0\!-\!1\!-\!2\!-\!3\!-\!4$ by the parity
bit $\ell(v)=(v\bmod 2)\in Q_1$. Each edge flips the one coordinate (edge-gentle),
yet $\ell(0)=\ell(2)=\ell(4)$, so $\dist_{Q_1}(\ell(0),\ell(4))=0<4=\dist_G(0,4)$:
the labeling contracts heavily but never stretches.

\section{Algorithms}\label{sec:alg}

Let $n=|V|$, $m=|E|$, $t$ the number of classes, and $k=t-\rank(A)$.

\paragraph{Computing labels.} Pick a spanning tree $T$ rooted at $r$; accumulate
class basis vectors along tree paths to get raw labels in $(\GF)^t$ in $O(nt)$
time. Non-tree edges yield a basis of $\mathcal{C}$; Gaussian elimination over
$\GF$ gives $\rank(A)$ and a surviving coordinate system, costing $O(mt^2/64)$
with bitset arithmetic. Project raw labels onto the $k$ surviving coordinates.

\paragraph{Hypercube distance.} By Theorem~\ref{thm:cube-dist},
$\dist_{Q_k}(x,y)=\Ham(x,y)=\mathrm{popcount}(x\oplus y)$, computable in $O(k)$
(or $O(k/64)$ with word-level operations).

\paragraph{Total defect.} Compute all-pairs graph distances by BFS from each
vertex ($O(nm)$), then sum $\dist_G(u,v)-\Ham(\ell(u),\ell(v))$ over pairs
($O(n^2 k)$). Theorem~\ref{thm:no-stretch} guarantees every summand is
nonnegative, doubling as a runtime sanity check.

\section{Discussion and future directions}

The No-Stretching Theorem isolates the unconditional half of the partial-cube
story, turning the distortion of a labeling into a single, always-nonnegative
number --- the contraction defect --- that can be summed, compared, and minimized.

\paragraph{A cycle-space formula.} We conjecture the total defect is zero exactly
when the partition refines the canonical relation grouping ``directly opposite''
edges, and in general is governed by the dimension of the cycle space the
partition fails to detect. The local, countable cycle-collapsing mechanism
suggests an exact bookkeeping formula.

\paragraph{Intrinsic partial cubes.} We conjecture a graph admits a zero-defect
partition iff it is a partial cube, with a unique coarsest such partition obtained
by merging classes whenever the merge preserves zero defect.

\paragraph{Random defects.} For bounded-degree graphs with edges colored into a
fixed number of classes uniformly at random, we conjecture the normalized defect
concentrates sharply around a value determined only by the degree distribution and
the number of classes, via martingale arguments on the abelian-group increments.

\section{Conclusion}

Any labeling of a connected graph into a binary hypercube that changes by at most
one coordinate along each edge is non-expansive: labeled distance never exceeds
graph distance. The proof reduces, through the identity that hypercube distance
equals Hamming distance, to a length-monotone push-forward of walks. The canonical
source of such labelings --- the parity quotient of an edge partition --- places
the result at the foundation of partial-cube theory, where it guarantees the
one-sided distortion bound unconditionally and recasts the residual distortion as
a well-behaved invariant ripe for further study.

    push-forward argument d_H(ell(u), ell(v)) <= d_G(u, v). When the class images
    are independent coordinate directions (e.g. the Djokovic-Winkler relation on a
    partial cube), H is exactly the standard Hamming hypercube and the two
    settings coincide.

The module is fully self-contained (standard library only), uses type hints, and
inlines every helper.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from collections import deque
from itertools import combinations
from typing import Dict, List, Set, Tuple

Vertex = int
Edge = Tuple[Vertex, Vertex]
Graph = Dict[Vertex, List[Vertex]]
BitVec = Tuple[int, ...]


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Hamming distance and the hypercube metric (Theorem: d_{Q_k} = Hamming).
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
def hamming_distance(x: BitVec, y: BitVec) -> int:
    """Number of coordinates in which two GF(2) vectors differ."""
    if len(x) != len(y):
        raise ValueError("vectors must have equal length")
    return sum(1 for a, b in zip(x, y) if a != b)


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Graph utilities.
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
def build_graph(n: int, edges: List[Edge]) -> Graph:
    """Adjacency-list undirected graph on vertices 0..n-1."""
    g: Graph = {v: [] for v in range(n)}
    for u, v in edges:
        g[u].append(v)
        g[v].append(u)
    return g


def bfs_distances(g: Graph, source: Vertex) -> Dict[Vertex, int]:
    """Single-source shortest-path distances by breadth-first search."""
    dist: Dict[Vertex, int] = {source: 0}
    queue: deque[Vertex] = deque([source])
    while queue:
        u = queue.popleft()
        for w in g[u]:
            if w not in dist:
                dist[w] = dist[u] + 1
                queue.append(w)
    return dist


def all_pairs_distances(g: Graph) -> Dict[Vertex, Dict[Vertex, int]]:
    """All-pairs shortest-path distances via repeated BFS."""
    return {v: bfs_distances(g, v) for v in g}


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# GF(2) linear algebra for the cycle space.
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
def gf2_row_reduce(rows: List[int]) -> List[int]:
    """Gaussian elimination over GF(2) on bitmask-encoded rows.

    Returns a list of pivot rows (a basis of the row space). Each row is an
    integer whose bit j is the j-th coordinate.
    """
    basis: List[int] = []
    for r in rows:
        cur = r
        for b in basis:
            cur = min(cur, cur ^ b)
        if cur:
            basis.append(cur)
            basis.sort(reverse=True)
    return basis


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Edge-gentleness check for a labeling into the Hamming hypercube.
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
def is_edge_gentle(edges: List[Edge], label: Dict[Vertex, BitVec]) -> bool:
    """True iff every edge has endpoints at Hamming distance 0 or 1."""
    return all(hamming_distance(label[u], label[v]) <= 1 for u, v in edges)


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# The edge-partition parity-quotient labeling (raw labels, quotient, generators).
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
def edge_partition_labeling(
    n: int,
    edges: List[Edge],
    edge_class: Dict[Edge, int],
    num_classes: int,
    root: Vertex = 0,
) -> Tuple[Dict[Vertex, BitVec], List[BitVec], int]:
    """Construct the parity-quotient labeling of vertices.

    Returns (label, generators, k):
      * label[v] : the k-bit quotient label of v (surviving coordinates),
      * generators : the images of the t edge classes in the quotient (the
        generating set of the Cayley graph H),
      * k = t - rank(A) : the quotient dimension.
    """
    g = build_graph(n, edges)

    def class_of(u: int, v: int) -> int:
        e = (u, v) if (u, v) in edge_class else (v, u)
        return edge_class[e]

    # 1. Raw labels via spanning-tree BFS; raw[v] is a bitmask over t classes.
    raw: Dict[Vertex, int] = {root: 0}
    tree_edges: Set[Edge] = set()
    queue: deque[Vertex] = deque([root])
    while queue:
        u = queue.popleft()
        for w in g[u]:
            if w not in raw:
                j = class_of(u, w)
                raw[w] = raw[u] ^ (1 << j)
                tree_edges.add((min(u, w), max(u, w)))
                queue.append(w)

    # 2. Cycle space: each non-tree edge {u,w} contributes raw[u] ^ raw[w] ^ e_j.
    cycle_rows: List[int] = []
    for u, v in edges:
        key = (min(u, v), max(u, v))
        if key in tree_edges:
            continue
        j = class_of(u, v)
        cycle_rows.append(raw[u] ^ raw[v] ^ (1 << j))
    basis = gf2_row_reduce(cycle_rows)
    rank_a = len(basis)

    # 3. Quotient: keep the non-pivot ("surviving") coordinates.
    pivot_coords = {b.bit_length() - 1 for b in basis}
    surviving = [j for j in range(num_classes) if j not in pivot_coords]

    def reduce_mod_cycle(vec: int) -> int:
        cur = vec
        for b in basis:
            cur = min(cur, cur ^ b)
        return cur

    def to_bits(vec: int) -> BitVec:
        reduced = reduce_mod_cycle(vec)
        return tuple((reduced >> j) & 1 for j in surviving)

    label: Dict[Vertex, BitVec] = {v: to_bits(raw[v]) for v in range(n)}
    generators = [to_bits(1 << j) for j in range(num_classes)]
    k = num_classes - rank_a
    return label, generators, k


def cayley_distances(k: int, generators: List[BitVec]) -> Dict[BitVec, int]:
    """Word-length distances from the identity in the Cayley graph on (Z/2)^k
    generated by `generators` (zero generators ignored). BFS over the group."""
    gens = [g for g in generators if any(g)]
    start: BitVec = tuple(0 for _ in range(k))
    dist: Dict[BitVec, int] = {start: 0}
    queue: deque[BitVec] = deque([start])
    while queue:
        x = queue.popleft()
        for g in gens:
            y = tuple(a ^ b for a, b in zip(x, g))
            if y not in dist:
                dist[y] = dist[x] + 1
                queue.append(y)
    return dist


def cayley_distance(
    a: BitVec, b: BitVec, cayley_from_id: Dict[BitVec, int]
) -> int:
    """Distance between two group elements = word length of their difference."""
    diff = tuple(x ^ y for x, y in zip(a, b))
    return cayley_from_id[diff]


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Verification routines.
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
def verify_no_stretching_hamming(
    n: int, edges: List[Edge], label: Dict[Vertex, BitVec]
) -> Tuple[bool, int]:
    """For an edge-gentle labeling: check Hamming(label) <= d_G everywhere.
    Returns (ok, total_defect) with total_defect = sum of (d_G - Hamming) >= 0."""
    dist = all_pairs_distances(build_graph(n, edges))
    ok, total_defect = True, 0
    for u, v in combinations(range(n), 2):
        dg, dh = dist[u][v], hamming_distance(label[u], label[v])
        ok = ok and (dh <= dg)
        total_defect += dg - dh
    return ok, total_defect


def verify_no_stretching_cayley(
    n: int,
    edges: List[Edge],
    label: Dict[Vertex, BitVec],
    k: int,
    generators: List[BitVec],
) -> Tuple[bool, int]:
    """For an edge-partition labeling: check d_H(label) <= d_G everywhere, where
    H is the Cayley graph generated by the class images."""
    dist = all_pairs_distances(build_graph(n, edges))
    cay = cayley_distances(k, generators)
    ok, total_defect = True, 0
    for u, v in combinations(range(n), 2):
        dg = dist[u][v]
        dh = cayley_distance(label[u], label[v], cay)
        ok = ok and (dh <= dg)
        total_defect += dg - dh
    return ok, total_defect


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Examples.
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
def example_cube_dist_equals_hamming() -> None:
    """Confirm d_{Q_k} = Hamming on random hypercube pairs (Q3)."""
    import random

    print("=" * 70)
    print("Example 1: hypercube distance equals Hamming distance (Q3)")
    random.seed(0)
    k = 3
    g = build_graph(
        2 ** k,
        [(x, x ^ (1 << i)) for x in range(2 ** k) for i in range(k)
         if x < (x ^ (1 << i))],
    )
    dist = all_pairs_distances(g)
    bits = lambda x: tuple((x >> i) & 1 for i in range(k))
    all_match = True
    for _ in range(6):
        a, b = random.randrange(2 ** k), random.randrange(2 ** k)
        gd, hd = dist[a][b], hamming_distance(bits(a), bits(b))
        all_match = all_match and (gd == hd)
        print(f"  x={bits(a)} y={bits(b)}  d_Q={gd}  Hamming={hd}")
    print(f"  all pairs match: {all_match}")


def example_edge_gentle_contraction() -> None:
    """A directly-defined edge-gentle labeling that strictly contracts.

    Path 0-1-2-3-4 labeled by parity ell(v) = (v mod 2) in Q1. Each edge flips the
    single coordinate (edge-gentle), but endpoints two apart collapse to equal
    labels: no-stretching holds and the defect is strictly positive."""
    print("=" * 70)
    print("Example 2: edge-gentle parity labeling of P5 into Q1 (core theorem)")
    n = 5
    edges: List[Edge] = [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4)]
    label: Dict[Vertex, BitVec] = {v: (v % 2,) for v in range(n)}
    for v in range(n):
        print(f"  label[{v}] = {label[v]}")
    print(f"  edge-gentle: {is_edge_gentle(edges, label)}")
    ok, defect = verify_no_stretching_hamming(n, edges, label)
    print(f"  no-stretching holds: {ok};  total contraction defect: {defect}")
    print("  (defect > 0  =>  the labeling genuinely contracts, never stretches)")


def example_partition_path() -> None:
    """Path P4, each edge its own class: isometric partial-cube embedding."""
    print("=" * 70)
    print("Example 3: edge partition of P4, each edge its own class")
    n = 4
    edges: List[Edge] = [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3)]
    edge_class = {(0, 1): 0, (1, 2): 1, (2, 3): 2}
    label, gens, k = edge_partition_labeling(n, edges, edge_class, 3)
    for v in range(n):
        print(f"  label[{v}] = {label[v]}")
    print(f"  quotient dimension k = {k};  class generators = {gens}")
    print(f"  edge-gentle (Hamming cube): {is_edge_gentle(edges, label)}")
    ok, defect = verify_no_stretching_cayley(n, edges, label, k, gens)
    print(f"  no-stretching (Cayley H) holds: {ok};  total defect: {defect}")
    print("  (defect 0  =>  isometric: P4 is a partial cube)")


def example_partition_c4() -> None:
    """4-cycle, Djokovic-Winkler partition: isometric into the Hamming cube Q2."""
    print("=" * 70)
    print("Example 4: Djokovic-Winkler partition of C4 (opposite edges paired)")
    n = 4
    edges: List[Edge] = [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 0)]
    edge_class = {(0, 1): 0, (2, 3): 0, (1, 2): 1, (3, 0): 1}
    label, gens, k = edge_partition_labeling(n, edges, edge_class, 2)
    for v in range(n):
        print(f"  label[{v}] = {label[v]}")
    print(f"  quotient dimension k = {k};  class generators = {gens}")
    print(f"  edge-gentle (Hamming cube): {is_edge_gentle(edges, label)}")
    ok, defect = verify_no_stretching_cayley(n, edges, label, k, gens)
    print(f"  no-stretching (Cayley H) holds: {ok};  total defect: {defect}")
    print("  (class images are standard basis  =>  H is the Hamming cube Q2)")


def example_partition_triangle() -> None:
    """Triangle K3: each edge its own class. The QUOTIENT labeling into the
    standard Hamming cube is NOT edge-gentle and would stretch; but the proper
    target is the Cayley graph H (here K4), in which no-stretching holds. This
    shows why the target generating set matters."""
    print("=" * 70)
    print("Example 5: triangle K3, each edge its own class")
    n = 3
    edges: List[Edge] = [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 0)]
    edge_class = {(0, 1): 0, (1, 2): 1, (2, 0): 2}
    label, gens, k = edge_partition_labeling(n, edges, edge_class, 3)
    for v in range(n):
        print(f"  label[{v}] = {label[v]}")
    print(f"  quotient dimension k = {k};  class generators = {gens}")
    print(f"  edge-gentle into standard Hamming cube: {is_edge_gentle(edges, label)}")
    ok_h, def_h = verify_no_stretching_hamming(n, edges, label)
    print(f"  -> standard Hamming cube: no-stretching holds: {ok_h} "
          f"(defect {def_h}; NEGATIVE means a STRETCH, hypothesis violated)")
    ok_c, def_c = verify_no_stretching_cayley(n, edges, label, k, gens)
    print(f"  -> Cayley graph H (K4): no-stretching holds: {ok_c} "
          f"(defect {def_c})")
    print("  (lesson: the no-stretching target is the Cayley graph of the class")
    print("   images; in the Hamming cube the labeling must first be edge-gentle)")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    example_cube_dist_equals_hamming()
    example_edge_gentle_contraction()
    example_partition_path()
    example_partition_c4()
    example_partition_triangle()
    print("=" * 70)
    print("All demonstrations complete.")

    class-parities of walks modulo the cycle space gives a labeling into the
    quotient (Z/2)^t / C, of dimension k = t - rank(A), where A is the
    cycle-class parity matrix over GF(2). Here the relevant target is the CAYLEY
    GRAPH H on the quotient group generated by the images of the t edge classes:
    every edge of G moves the label by exactly one generator, so by the same
    push-forward argument d_H(ell(u), ell(v)) <= d_G(u, v). When the class images
    are independent coordinate directions (e.g. the Djokovic-Winkler relation on a

        g[v].append(u)

                dist[w] = dist[u] + 1

    n: int,

    edge_class: Dict[Edge, int],

    root: Vertex = 0,

    raw: Dict[Vertex, int] = {root: 0}

    queue: deque[Vertex] = deque([root])
    while queue:
        u = queue.popleft()
        for w in g[u]:
            if w not in raw:
                j = class_of(u, w)
                raw[w] = raw[u] ^ (1 << j)
                tree_edges.add((min(u, w), max(u, w)))

    gens = [g for g in generators if any(g)]

    while queue:
        x = queue.popleft()
        for g in gens:
            y = tuple(a ^ b for a, b in zip(x, g))
            if y not in dist:
                dist[y] = dist[x] + 1
                queue.append(y)

    a: BitVec, b: BitVec, cayley_from_id: Dict[BitVec, int]

    diff = tuple(x ^ y for x, y in zip(a, b))

    dist = all_pairs_distances(build_graph(n, edges))

    return ok, total_defect


def verify_no_stretching_cayley(
    n: int,
    edges: List[Edge],
    label: Dict[Vertex, BitVec],
    k: int,
    generators: List[BitVec],
) -> Tuple[bool, int]:
    """For an edge-partition labeling: check d_H(label) <= d_G everywhere, where
    H is the Cayley graph generated by the class images."""
    dist = all_pairs_distances(build_graph(n, edges))
    cay = cayley_distances(k, generators)
    ok, total_defect = True, 0
    for u, v in combinations(range(n), 2):
        dg = dist[u][v]

        total_defect += dg - dh
    return ok, total_defect


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Examples.
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
def example_cube_dist_equals_hamming() -> None:
    """Confirm d_{Q_k} = Hamming on random hypercube pairs (Q3)."""
    import random

    print("=" * 70)
    print("Example 1: hypercube distance equals Hamming distance (Q3)")
    random.seed(0)
    k = 3
    g = build_graph(
        2 ** k,
        [(x, x ^ (1 << i)) for x in range(2 ** k) for i in range(k)

    )

        print(f"  x={bits(a)} y={bits(b)}  d_Q={gd}  Hamming={hd}")
    print(f"  all pairs match: {all_match}")


def example_edge_gentle_contraction() -> None:
    """A directly-defined edge-gentle labeling that strictly contracts.

    Path 0-1-2-3-4 labeled by parity ell(v) = (v mod 2) in Q1. Each edge flips the
    single coordinate (edge-gentle), but endpoints two apart collapse to equal
    labels: no-stretching holds and the defect is strictly positive."""
    print("=" * 70)
    print("Example 2: edge-gentle parity labeling of P5 into Q1 (core theorem)")

    label: Dict[Vertex, BitVec] = {v: (v % 2,) for v in range(n)}

algorithms.name: Parity-Quotient Labeling from an Edge Partition over GF(2)
algorithms.description: Constructs the vertex labeling induced by an edge partition. Raw labels are accumulated along a spanning tree (one class basis vector per traversed edge); the cycle-class parity vectors of the non-tree edges span the cycle space, whose GF(2) rank is obtained by Gaussian elimination on bitmask rows. Quotienting by the cycle space yields labels in dimension k = t - rank(A), together with the class generators of the resulting Cayley target. Complexity: O(n*t) for raw labels, O(m*t^2/64) for the bitset elimination, O(n*t) for projection.
algorithms.pseudocode:
Input: graph G=(V,E), edge->class map c, t classes, root r
1. BFS a spanning tree T from r; raw[r] := 0
2. for each tree edge (u,w) in BFS order: raw[w] := raw[u] XOR e_{c(u,w)}
3. for each non-tree edge {u,v}: add raw[u] XOR raw[v] XOR e_{c(u,v)} to cycle_rows
4. basis := GF(2) row-reduce(cycle_rows); rank_A := |basis|
5. pivots := {highest set bit of each basis row}; surviving := classes not in pivots
6. for each vertex v: reduce raw[v] modulo basis, then read off surviving coordinates -> label[v]
7. generators[j] := reduce(e_j) read off surviving coordinates
Output: label, generators, k = t - rank_A

algorithms.name: Cayley-Graph Word-Length Distance on the Quotient Group
algorithms.description: Computes shortest-path distance in the Cayley graph H on (Z/2)^k generated by the class images. Because each graph edge moves the label by exactly one generator, this is the target metric for which the no-stretching bound holds for arbitrary edge partitions. A single BFS from the identity over the 2^k group elements yields the word length of every element; the distance between two labels is the word length of their XOR. Complexity: O(2^k * |generators|).
algorithms.pseudocode:
Input: dimension k, generator set S (drop zero vectors)
1. dist[0^k] := 0; queue := [0^k]
2. while queue nonempty:
3.   x := dequeue
4.   for g in S: y := x XOR g; if y unseen: dist[y] := dist[x]+1; enqueue y
5. distance(a,b) := dist[a XOR b]
Output: dist table; distance(a,b)
algorithms.code:
from collections import deque
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple

BitVec = Tuple[int, ...]


def cayley_distances(k: int, generators: List[BitVec]) -> Dict[BitVec, int]:
    """Word-length distances from the identity in the Cayley graph on (Z/2)^k
    generated by `generators`, computed by BFS over the 2^k group elements."""
    gens = [g for g in generators if any(g)]
    start: BitVec = tuple(0 for _ in range(k))
    dist: Dict[BitVec, int] = {start: 0}
    q: deque[BitVec] = deque([start])
    while q:
        x = q.popleft()
        for g in gens:
            y = tuple(a ^ b for a, b in zip(x, g))
            if y not in dist:
                dist[y] = dist[x] + 1
                q.append(y)
    return dist


def cayley_distance(a: BitVec, b: BitVec, cayley_from_id: Dict[BitVec, int]) -> int:
    """Distance between two group elements = word length of their difference."""
    return cayley_from_id[tuple(x ^ y for x, y in zip(a, b))]

algorithms.name: Total Contraction Defect of a Labeling
algorithms.description: Aggregates the one-sided distortion of an edge-gentle labeling into a single nonnegative invariant by summing, over all unordered vertex pairs, the difference between graph distance (all-pairs BFS) and Hamming distance of the labels. The No-Stretching Theorem guarantees every summand is nonnegative; a negative summand certifies a bug (or a non-edge-gentle labeling). The defect is zero exactly for isometric (partial-cube) labelings. Complexity: O(n*m) for all-pairs distances plus O(n^2 * k) for the summation.
algorithms.pseudocode:
Input: graph G, labeling label
1. for each vertex s: D[s] := BFS distances from s
2. total := 0
3. for each unordered pair {u,v}: total += D[u][v] - Hamming(label[u], label[v])
Output: total  (>= 0 by the No-Stretching Theorem)

visualizations.name: No-Stretching Scatter: Labeled Distance vs Graph Distance
visualizations.description: For a sample graph and an edge-gentle labeling, plots every vertex pair as a point (graph distance, labeled distance). The No-Stretching Theorem forces all points onto or below the diagonal, which the plot shades as the admissible region. Points strictly below the diagonal are contracted (shortcut) pairs.

"""Visualization: contraction defect of a labeling versus graph distance.

Plots, for a sample graph and an edge-gentle labeling, every pair (d_G, d_Q) as a
scatter point. The No-Stretching Theorem forces all points onto or below the
diagonal d_Q = d_G: the labeling never stretches. Requires matplotlib.
"""
from collections import deque
from itertools import combinations
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def bfs(adj, src):
    dist = {src: 0}
    q = deque([src])
    while q:
        u = q.popleft()
        for w in adj[u]:
            if w not in dist:
                dist[w] = dist[u] + 1
                q.append(w)
    return dist


def main():
    # A 6-cycle with a "folding" parity labeling into Q1 (v mod 2).
    n = 6
    edges = [(i, (i + 1) % n) for i in range(n)]
    adj = {v: [] for v in range(n)}
    for u, v in edges:
        adj[u].append(v); adj[v].append(u)
    label = {v: (v % 2,) for v in range(n)}
    dmat = {v: bfs(adj, v) for v in range(n)}

    xs, ys = [], []
    for u, v in combinations(range(n), 2):
        xs.append(dmat[u][v])
        ys.append(sum(1 for a, b in zip(label[u], label[v]) if a != b))

    lim = max(xs) + 1
    plt.figure(figsize=(6, 6))
    plt.plot([0, lim], [0, lim], "k--", label="$d_Q = d_G$ (isometry)")
    plt.fill_between([0, lim], [0, lim], 0, alpha=0.1, color="green",
                     label="no-stretching region $d_Q \\leq d_G$")
    plt.scatter(xs, ys, s=80, c="crimson", zorder=3, label="vertex pairs")
    plt.xlabel("graph distance $d_G(u,v)$")
    plt.ylabel("labeled distance $d_Q(\\ell u,\\ell v)$")
    plt.title("No-Stretching: all pairs lie on or below the diagonal")
    plt.legend(); plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
    plt.savefig("no_stretching_scatter.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
    print("saved no_stretching_scatter.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

import Mathlib

/-! # No-stretching for labelings into the hypercube over GF(2)

Let `G` be a connected simple graph on `V`, and `ℓ : V → (Fin k → ZMod 2)` a labeling such that
every `G`-edge `{u,v}` satisfies either `ℓ u = ℓ v` or `HammingDist (ℓ u) (ℓ v) = 1`.

We prove that such a labeling does not stretch distances: the hypercube distance between labels is
bounded by the graph distance.
-/

open SimpleGraph

namespace HypercubeNoStretch

abbrev Cube (k : ℕ) := Fin k → ZMod 2

def HammingDist {k : ℕ} (x y : Cube k) : ℕ :=
  (Finset.univ.filter (fun i => x i ≠ y i)).card

def hypercube (k : ℕ) : SimpleGraph (Cube k) :=
  SimpleGraph.fromRel (fun x y => HammingDist x y = 1)

theorem hypercube_dist_eq_hammingDist {k : ℕ} (x y : Cube k) :
    (hypercube k).dist x y = HammingDist x y := by sorry

theorem exists_image_walk {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V} {k : ℕ} {ℓ : V → Cube k}
    (hℓ : ∀ {u v : V}, G.Adj u v → ℓ u = ℓ v ∨ HammingDist (ℓ u) (ℓ v) = 1)
    {u v : V} (w : G.Walk u v) :
    ∃ w' : (hypercube k).Walk (ℓ u) (ℓ v), w'.length ≤ w.length := by sorry

theorem no_stretching {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V} {k : ℕ} {ℓ : V → Cube k}
    (hG : G.Connected)
    (hℓ : ∀ {u v : V}, G.Adj u v → ℓ u = ℓ v ∨ HammingDist (ℓ u) (ℓ v) = 1)
    (u v : V) :
    (hypercube k).dist (ℓ u) (ℓ v) ≤ G.dist u v := by sorry

end HypercubeNoStretch

# Future Directions — One-Sided Distance Distortion of Edge-Partition Labelings

The central finding of this cycle is sharp and one-sided: the parity labeling attached to any
edge partition of a connected graph contracts distances but never expands them. The slack
between the graph distance and the image distance is therefore a genuine, always-nonnegative
*defect* — a quantity worth studying in its own right. The conjectures below grow directly out
of that observation and the small-case experiments that accompanied it.

## Conjecture 1 — The contraction defect is a partition invariant with a cycle-space formula

For a fixed graph, define the total defect of a partition as the sum over all vertex pairs of
the difference between the graph distance and the labeled distance. We conjecture that this
defect is zero exactly when the partition refines the canonical relation that groups edges
lying "directly opposite" across the graph, and that in general it is governed by the dimension
of the cycle space the partition fails to detect.

The key insight is that every unit of defect is created by a closed walk whose class-parities
cancel, so the defect counts, with multiplicity, the cycles the partition collapses rather than
resolves. **Why now?** The construction makes the cycle-collapsing mechanism explicit and
local (one edge moves the label by one direction), turning a global metric comparison into a
countable bookkeeping of cancellations, which is precisely the kind of object a defect formula
can pin down.

## Conjecture 2 — Coarsest zero-defect partition characterizes partial cubes intrinsically

A graph admits an edge partition with zero contraction defect if and only if it is a partial
cube, and among all such partitions there is a unique coarsest one, obtained by merging classes
whenever doing so preserves zero defect.

The key insight is that the no-stretching bound already gives one inequality for free, so being
a partial cube is *equivalent* to closing the remaining gap, and gap-closing is monotone under
merging compatible classes. **Why now?** With the contraction direction settled
unconditionally, the only obstruction left to isometry is a single, testable equality, making a
clean lattice of "good" partitions tractable for the first time.

## Conjecture 3 — Random edge partitions concentrate their defect

If the edges of a bounded-degree graph are colored into a fixed number of classes uniformly at
random, the normalized contraction defect concentrates sharply around a deterministic value
determined only by the degree distribution and the number of classes.

The key insight is that the per-edge increment is an independent draw from a small group, so the
labeled distance is a sum of weakly dependent steps whose fluctuations are controlled by
martingale arguments. **Why now?** The labeling reduces a metric question to a random-walk
question on an abelian group, exactly the setting where modern concentration tools are at their
most powerful.
